pullRequest.title: gtk: implement GtkAccessibleText for the terminal surface
pullRequest.body:
This PR is a first step toward making Ghostty usable for blind users on Linux.

Screen reader accessibility was requested in
https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/2351. I opened a vouch
request for this work in
https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/13746, which jcollie
granted. The staged PR order described there starts with this
one.

### What this PR does

With this change the Orca screen reader can read the terminal viewport: the
visible text, the cursor position, hit-testing between screen points and text
offsets, per-row rectangles so flat review works, and change events as output
arrives so Orca can announce what changed.

### What it contains

- `src/apprt/a11y_text.zig` and `src/apprt/a11y_offsets.zig`: the snapshot
  walk and the offset math. Both are GTK-free and unit tested.
- `src/benchmark/A11yText.zig`: a benchmark for the snapshot walk and for the
  per-frame change probe.
- The `GtkAccessibleText` implementation on `GhosttySurface`.
- Application and window identity for AT-SPI, so the window is announced with
  a name and the right role instead of as an unnamed object.

### Performance

The per-frame work is a cheap change probe, not a rebuild: 6.7us at 30x80 and
17.6us at 60x200. A full snapshot rebuild costs 9.5us and 23.2us respectively
and only runs when the probe reports that the contents actually changed.

To reproduce, against a ReleaseFast build:

    ghostty-gen +styled --seed=42 --style-rate=0.3 | head -c 4000000 > corpus
    ghostty-bench +a11y-text --mode=probe --terminal-rows=30 \
        --terminal-cols=80 --loops=1000 --data=corpus

Those figures are hyperfine medians over 10 runs after 3 warmups.

The probe only runs once an AT client has queried the surface at least once,
and only on frames that surface actually renders, so an idle terminal and a
terminal nobody is inspecting both cost nothing.

I deliberately did not gate this on focus. With splits, that would silence a
build running in the other half of the window. Whether to speak an unfocused
terminal is the AT client's policy call, not ours to pre-empt by withholding
the events. There is a comment in `glareaRender` explaining this, and why
`org.a11y.Status.IsEnabled` is not the gate it looks like either.

### GTK versions

`get_extents` and `get_offset` were added to `GtkAccessibleTextInterface` in
GTK 4.16. `G_DEFINE_INTERFACE` allocates the vtable at the running GTK's
`sizeof`, so writing those two slots unconditionally would write past the
allocation on an older runtime. They are installed only when the running GTK
is 4.16 or newer. Everything else in the interface is 4.14, and the public
wrappers for those two null-check, so on 4.14 they simply do not participate.

### Testing

48 unit tests across the two new modules, 42 of them in `a11y_offsets.zig`.

The one that matters most is a 3000 iteration round-trip fuzz test. It replays
the change events we emit against a model of the AT client's own copy of the
text and asserts the two never diverge. That test is why I trust the diff.

Beyond the unit tests I have been driving this daily with Orca and a braille
display.

### One thing I cannot test myself

I am blind, so I cannot verify mouse behaviour.

The change I would most like a sighted reviewer to look at is
`src/apprt/gtk/ui/1.2/surface.blp`: focus and both event controllers move from
the inner `GLArea` up to `GhosttySurface`. That move is what makes the surface
an accessible focus target, but it is also the part of this diff most likely
to break things for sighted users. The four things need checking:

1. Clicking a surface focuses it.
2. Click-drag selection copies to PRIMARY.
3. Middle-click pastes.
4. Clicking an unfocused split focuses it.

### What is not in this PR

Selection, text attributes, and links, in that order.

### Test harness

I have an end-to-end harness on my `gtk-accessibility-poc` branch: pytest
driving a real Ghostty window over AT-SPI under Xvfb. 41 tests, 36 of them
passing against this branch; the 5 failures are all features deferred to the
later PRs (attributes, selection, set_caret).

I left it out here because it needs a display server, so it would have to be
opt-in and disabled in CI, the same shape as the existing macOS XCUITest
suite. Happy to submit it separately if you want it.

## AI Usage Disclosure

This change was developed with heavy assistance from Claude Code (Anthropic). I direct the design and behavior and Claude Code writes most of the Zig under my review. All code was reviewed, built, and tested by me before submission, including daily use with Orca and a braille display.

I think we should do some benchmarking on this. Christian Hergert added accessibility to VTE and he found there to be a drop in performance with accessibility enabled. The drop was large enough that accessibility is disabled by default in Ptyxis, if I remember correctly.

I see you already did some performance work, but it isn't clear if there is a degradation in performance. Maybe I cannot read!

performance was one of my concerns from the start (Exactly because I'm a long time VTE user). that is why this PR ships a benchmark commit (ghostty-bench +a11y-text) next to the feature and why the change events are gated the way they are.

the cost has three levels:

1. no AT client: the per frame hook sets one boolean and returns. nothing is walked. the code only becomes active after a real AT-SPI client reads the surface once. so for users without a screen reader there is no measurable degradation, and no need for an off by default switch.

2. AT client attached, frame rendered but nothing changed. this is the number that matters most because it is paid on every rendered frame while orca is running, and it runs under the renderer mutex, so it is the one that could hurt io throughput. it is a text only walk into a retained buffer plus a memcmp. i used claude to measure it today with hyperfine, 100k iterations, noop mode subtracted: 4.0 us per frame at 30x80 and 12.6 us at 60x200. at 60 fps that is under 0.1 percent of the frame budget.

3. AT client attached and the frame changed: full rebuild with cell widths, 5.3 us at 30x80 and 15.2 us at 60x200, plus change events. the events are diffed to the smallest remove and insert pair, so a keystroke emits a few characters, not the whole viewport. emitting the whole viewport every frame is the classic way a terminal kills both performance and the screen reader, so that was gated from day one.

i asked claude to read And compare the VTE implementation With our accessibility implementation and here their reply verbatim:

> What VTE does (vteaccess-gtk4.cc, current master):
>
> _vte_accessible_text_init() is called from the widget's constructed() (in GTK4 builds with a11y compiled in) and connects to the terminal's contents-changed signal. Every emission of that signal runs vte_accessible_text_contents_snapshot(), which rebuilds the entire accessibility state:
>
> - the viewport text, via get_text_displayed_a11y(), which also fills a VteCharAttributes record (row, column, foreground and background color resolved per cell, underline, strikethrough) for every byte of the text (vte_char_attr_list_fill);
> - a byte-offset array with one entry per character;
> - a linebreak scan that touches one attribute record per character;
> - an O(n) loop over every character to locate the caret (vte_accessible_text_contents_find_caret);
> - a fresh GString and GBytes allocation each time.
>
> At 60x200 the attribute list alone is hundreds of kilobytes written per content change. The change events themselves are diffed to a minimal prefix/suffix range, so the event side is reasonable; the cost is in the snapshot that precedes the diff.
>
> The gate for all of this is vte_terminal_get_enable_a11y(), a config property whose default is true (vtegtk.cc, enable-a11y param spec). There is no check for whether an AT client is actually connected. GTK itself drops the event emission when no AT context is realized, but by that point the snapshot work has already been done. So with default settings, every VTE terminal pays
> the full snapshot cost on every content change even when nothing is listening on the accessibility bus. That is consistent with the performance drop Christian observed and with why a user-facing switch exists and Ptyxis ships with it off.
>
> How this PR differs:
>
> - The gate is client activity, not configuration. The per-frame hook stores one boolean until the first real AT-SPI read latches the surface active (frameRendered in surface_a11y.zig). No screen reader means no walk, ever, so no switch is needed.
> - The per-frame path while a reader is attached builds text only: no attributes, no color resolution, no per-character arrays, and no allocation in steady state (a retained probe buffer plus a memcmp).
> - The caret position falls out of the same walk that builds the text, instead of a separate O(n) search afterward.
> - Cell widths are recorded only on frames that actually changed, and text attributes are not collected at all in this PR. The follow-up that adds them computes them on demand inside the get_attributes query, where the AT asks about one position at a time, rather than per frame.
>
> The measured numbers above (4 to 13 us per unchanged frame) are the direct consequence of that structure: the per-frame work is a fraction of a percent of a 60 fps frame budget, and only exists while a screen reader is actually attached.

as a blind person who relies on accessibility every day, to be honest: i am not very comfortable with gating a11y behind a config option the way VTE does. it is obscure for the people who need it most, and IMHO it sends the wrong signal.

in defense of the client attachment approach: it is a well proven path. Chromium and Firefox both enable their accessibility engines only when an assistive technology client actually shows up, for the same reason.

hello @mitchellh thanks for looking into it.

yes, i looked at the formatter. it was the first thing i studied, through the macOS path (ghostty_surface_read_text -> dumpText -> selectionString -> ScreenFormatter). the snapshot walk should still be reference it in a comment: interior blanks are kept as spaces the same way ScreenFormatter keeps non trailing blanks.

the reason i did not build on it is that AT-SPI needs a different output contract than a formatted string:

1. line identity. in the snapshot, line i of the text is always viewport row i. an empty row still contributes its newline (there is a test for this). the formatter's plain mode elides blank rows until a non blank one follows and drops trailing blank rows completely, and selectionString hardcodes unwrap=true, so soft wrapped rows are joined into one line. all the offset math on top (per line extents, point to offset, caret routing, orca flat review reading "line n") relies on line == row.

2. units. AT-SPI speaks codepoint offsets and screen columns. the snapshot records one width byte per codepoint (2 for a wide cell, 0 for a combining mark, 1 otherwise), and only the cell walk can produce that, because it is what sees cell.wide. the formatter's answer to position mapping is PinMap/PointMap, which map byte to pin, are documented as a significant performance hit, answer the inverse question, and would still need byte to codepoint and pin to viewport row conversion on every AT query.

3. the caret. the cursor offset falls out of the same walk. the formatter can only express the cursor as a CUP escape in vt mode, so with plain output i would need an O(n) scan afterwards, which is exactly the VTE find_caret slow pattern from my previous comment.

4. the per frame probe writes into a retained buffer with no allocation while holding the renderer mutex. to be fair, this one is not fundamental: the formatter has a fast run path and could probably be made comparably fast (at least claude thinks so last time i explored it). the mismatch is the contract here.

retrofitting that onto the formatter means adding a11y only options to a general purpose tool used for copy, vt and html: keep blank rows, a widths sidecar, codepoint counting, a cursor out parameter. a self contained walk with its own tests and benchmark felt smaller and safer. but i am not attached to the split: if after a deeper look you would rather see this as a formatter mode (a "grid" emit variant), i am happy to rework it that way. the GTK caching layer does not care where the bytes come from.

on the utf8 point: agreed. the generic part is three small helpers at the top of offsets.zig  and utf8CpCount is just a wrapper over simd.countUtf8. i can move them into src/unicode right away. the rest of offsets.zig is a11y specific offset math (codepoint boundary aligned diffing, grid to offset mapping, granularity queries for get_string_at_offset). i checked and I think there is nothing similar elsewhere in the tree to reuse.

the package location is also not something i am attached to. the only hard requirement i Imagine. is that the walk stays outside the GTK class so it can be unit tested and benchmarked without a live GTK surface and an AT-SPI bus. root level src/a11y was my choice for that, but src/terminal or anywhere else works too. long term it could also serve the macOS side: the formatter string works there because VoiceOver pulls a whole string on demand, but for example accessibilityLine(for:) currently re-derives line structure by splitting that string on every query, which is the kind of work the snapshot plus offsets design exists to avoid.

## Pull request overview Implements initial AT-SPI text accessibility for the GTK terminal surface by exposing terminal viewport text, caret position, hit-testing, per-line extents, and incremental change events through `GtkAccessibleText`, backed by GTK-free snapshot/diff logic that is unit-tested and benchmarked. **Changes:** - Add GTK-independent viewport snapshot builder (`a11y_text`) and offset/diff math (`a11y_offsets`), with extensive unit tests. - Implement `GtkAccessibleText` (+ `GtkAccessible` override) on `GhosttySurface`, including cached snapshots, change probing, and AT-SPI update signals. - Add an `a11y-text` benchmark and seed app/window accessibility identity and roles for better screen reader discovery. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 11 out of 11 changed files in this pull request and generated 3 comments.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | src/build/SharedDeps.zig | Adds `graphene` pkg-config mapping needed for `graphene.Point/Rect` usage in accessibility APIs. | | src/benchmark/main.zig | Exposes the new `A11yText` benchmark module. | | src/benchmark/cli.zig | Registers the `a11y-text` benchmark action and wiring. | | src/benchmark/A11yText.zig | Adds benchmark for snapshot build vs per-frame probe paths. | | src/apprt/gtk/ui/1.2/surface.blp | Moves focus/key controllers to `GhosttySurface` to make the accessible terminal object the focus target. | | src/apprt/gtk/class/window.zig | Seeds `accessible-role=window` at construct time for correct AT-SPI role reporting. | | src/apprt/gtk/class/surface.zig | Implements `GtkAccessibleText` and associated caching/probing/diff-based update emissions on the surface. | | src/apprt/gtk/class/application.zig | Seeds prgname/application name early and ensures quick-terminal windows also get `accessible-role=window`. | | src/apprt/a11y_text.zig | New GTK-free viewport snapshot builder (text + optional per-codepoint cell widths) with unit tests. | | src/apprt/a11y_offsets.zig | New GTK-free offset math + minimal diff selection with extensive tests and fuzz-style round-trip validation. | | src/apprt.zig | Includes new modules in the test build. |

`finalize` deinitializes the ArrayLists but never frees `ax_cached_text` or `ax_last_snapshot` when they are still populated, which leaks heap allocations (both are allocated via `std.heap.c_allocator` in `axRefreshCache` / `axNotifyIfChanged`). These buffers are not owned by GTK long-term (callbacks wrap slices into freshly-allocated `GBytes`), so they should be freed during finalize as well.

The doc comment for `axRefreshCache` says it "Uses a 500ms cache", but the implementation is frame/staleness-based (serves the cache until a rendered frame marks it stale and it gets rebuilt on demand). This mismatch makes it harder to reason about when the renderer mutex may be taken.

If the cursor lands on a `.spacer_tail` cell (the second half of a wide character), `cell.hasText()` is false and the current logic treats it like a blank run. Because spacer cells are skipped and don't increment `blank_cells`, `cursor_blank_idx` never resolves and the cursor ends up anchored to end-of-row, even when there is text after the wide character. Special-case spacer cells so the cursor byte offset resolves to `snap.end()` (i.e. immediately after the wide character already emitted).

Indeed good ideas, thanks. Done both.

utf8CpLen is now a wrapper over std.unicode.utf8ByteSequenceLength. We cannot use the std counting functions like utf8CountCodepoints directly because they return errors and the accessibility callbacks don't have a good error path.

Regarding simdutf, we now use it for utf8CpCount when it is available (scalar fallback otherwise). I benchmarked it: 44-59x faster than the scalar loop on viewport sized buffers (20-83ns vs 0.9-4.9us). So definitely thank you for pushing me in the right direction here.

Fully agree. moved to a new src/a11y package (main.zig, text.zig, offsets.zig). I picked src/a11y over src/terminal because the units here (AT-SPI codepoint offsets, widget space points) are accessibility concepts, not terminal ones, and later PRs in this series (links, attributes) will add more runtime independent logic there.
More idiomatic Zig here would use a `*std.Io.Writer` so this function remains reusable for all buffer impls, but it's a fairly minor detail
